title: Tensor Parallelism
subtitle: Topic: Tensor Parallelism · Subject: Distributed AI Training · Seven questions, custom diagrams, and a PyTorch DeviceMesh example.

TENSOR PARALLELISM · DISTRIBUTED AI TRAINING

Split one layer across several GPUs

Share oversized weight matrices and coordinate partial calculations using collective communication.

questions.stem: What is Tensor Parallelism in Distributed AI Training, and how does it divide the computation of one neural-network layer across multiple GPUs?
options: Tensor Parallelism divides the calculations of a large layer among GPUs, but every GPU must store the full weight matrix. Only input examples are partitioned, so the layer's memory requirement is not reduced and its weights remain replicated.

Tensor Parallelism splits the weights and calculations of a single neural-network layer across multiple GPUs. Each GPU computes a shard of the layer, and communication combines or redistributes results so the distributed model works together.

Tensor Parallelism partitions a layer's weights across devices and lets each GPU produce a partial output. Those pieces count as complete independent predictions without communication or redistribution between devices, even in subsequent layers.

Tensor Parallelism assigns separate complete network layers to different GPUs and passes activations from one layer to the next. Each layer's weight matrix stays intact on the GPU executing it instead of being split among workers.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Tensor Parallelism (TP) divides the weights and calculations inside one large layer across GPUs. Each device handles a shard, not a complete copy. Depending on the layout, workers may gather output slices or reduce partial sums before the next operation. For example, a language model's oversized feed-forward projection can be shared between two GPUs when it will not fit on one. TP reduces per-GPU weight storage but requires communication to keep the distributed computation consistent.

questions.stem: Why can Tensor Parallelism help train a large language model whose linear layers do not fit on one GPU, and what does each GPU store and compute?
options: Each GPU stores a full copy of the oversized layer and processes different training examples. This reduces the model-weight memory needed by each GPU while keeping every gradient update independent of the other workers.

Each GPU holds a different weight shard, but all shards operate on separate training targets and never exchange results. The final language model is assembled only after the entire training run is finished, without intermediate coordination.

Each GPU stores one complete layer from the model's depth and forwards its output to another stage. This reduces memory for the oversized linear layer itself because that same layer is automatically divided into smaller pieces.

Each GPU stores a different shard of an oversized layer's weights and computes the matching output slice or partial sum. This reduces memory per GPU, while exchanging required results introduces communication overhead between devices.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A large language model can contain weight matrices too big for one accelerator, especially when gradients and optimizer states also use memory. Tensor Parallelism distributes a matrix across GPUs, and each GPU computes the output slice or partial sum for its own shard. For example, four GPUs may store four output-feature portions of a transformer projection. Those portions can remain partitioned for a following operation or be combined when required. Memory is shared across devices, but collective communication adds cost.

questions.stem: How is Tensor Parallelism different from Data Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism when distributing a neural network for training?
options: Tensor Parallelism splits computations within a layer across GPUs. Data Parallelism replicates the model to train on different data batches, while Pipeline Parallelism assigns different layers to stages. Large training systems can combine these strategies.

Tensor Parallelism copies all model weights to every GPU and divides training batches, while Data Parallelism distributes individual weight matrices. Pipeline Parallelism places complete layers in consecutive execution stages with no copies of those matrices.

Tensor Parallelism assigns consecutive complete network layers to different stages, while Pipeline Parallelism divides each weight matrix between GPUs. Data Parallelism keeps full model copies processing separate training examples rather than splitting individual layers.

Tensor Parallelism splits one layer among GPUs, while Data Parallelism distributes different examples among workers. Pipeline Parallelism also divides those examples between replicas instead of placing different model layers on separate stages.
questions.explanation: Explanation: These three methods split different parts of training. TP partitions computations inside a layer. Data Parallelism replicates the model and processes different batches; its gradients must be synchronized. Pipeline Parallelism places consecutive model layers on distinct stages. Imagine a satellite-image model trained on many GPUs: separate data workers classify different batches, a wide layer spans two GPUs, and deep layer groups run in a pipeline. Hybrid training combines these patterns, but each introduces different data movement and scheduling.

questions.stem: How do column-wise and row-wise Tensor Parallelism split a linear layer, and why may the GPUs need all-gather or all-reduce communication?
options: Column-wise sharding divides input features and adds partial sums, while row-wise sharding divides output features into independent slices. All-gather averages gradients, and all-reduce combines only input data before a layer begins.

Column-wise and row-wise sharding both divide the model by output features, but row-wise copies its weight shards to every GPU. All-gather and all-reduce are needed only for checkpoint saving, not during forward computation.

Column-wise sharding divides output features, giving GPUs different output slices. Row-wise sharding divides input features, so each GPU calculates a partial contribution that may need summation. All-gather assembles shards; all-reduce combines partial sums.

Column-wise sharding creates output slices and row-wise sharding creates input contributions, but the next unsharded layer can always execute without exchanging results at all. Collective communication is necessary only when GPUs process different data batches.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A linear layer maps input features to output features. Column-wise TP gives different output features to GPUs, producing output slices. Row-wise TP partitions the input-feature dimension, so workers calculate partial contributions to the same outputs; these often need summation. All-gather makes shards available together, while all-reduce sums contributions across ranks. For example, a text encoder might distribute eight output channels as four per GPU. Exactly where communication occurs depends on how the next layer expects its activations.

questions.stem: How can PyTorch apply Tensor Parallelism to a small two-layer network using DeviceMesh, ColwiseParallel, RowwiseParallel, and parallelize_module?
options: Start one process per GPU and create a DeviceMesh, but call parallelize_module without a parallelization plan. The API will automatically find large layers and shard them using both column-wise and row-wise strategies before any forward pass starts.

Start one distributed process per GPU, create a one-dimensional DeviceMesh, and call parallelize_module with ColwiseParallel on the first linear layer and RowwiseParallel on the second. The runtime manages the planned parameter shards and communication.

Build one complete model on each GPU and use a DeviceMesh, but apply ColwiseParallel only after training when merging optimizer states. The linear layers remain unsharded during forward and backward passes, so workers perform identical dense computations.

Create a one-dimensional DeviceMesh and apply ColwiseParallel to both linear layers, assuming their output layouts always match the next layer's input. No redistribution or reduction is required between devices, regardless of the adjoining layers.
questions.explanation: Explanation: PyTorch uses a one-dimensional DeviceMesh to describe the tensor-parallel GPU group. With parallelize_module, a plan can assign ColwiseParallel to the first Linear layer and RowwiseParallel to the second, keeping their intermediate features sharded. The short example below uses a two-GPU job, where each process selects its local device. For example, a small 8-to-16-to-8 model demonstrates the same structure used for much wider transformer layers. Check your PyTorch version, since these tensor-parallel APIs are experimental.

05 · VISUAL LESSON

A two-GPU DeviceMesh plan

PyTorch · 2-GPU tensor parallelism13 lines
01 import os, torch
02 from torch import nn
03 from torch.distributed.device_mesh import init_device_mesh
04 from torch.distributed.tensor.parallel import (
05     ColwiseParallel, RowwiseParallel, parallelize_module)
06 torch.distributed.init_process_group("nccl")
07 torch.cuda.set_device(int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]))
08 mesh = init_device_mesh("cuda", (torch.distributed.get_world_size(),))
09 net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(8,16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16,8)).cuda()
10 net = parallelize_module(net, mesh, {
11     "0": ColwiseParallel(), "2": RowwiseParallel()})
12 x = torch.randn(2, 8, device="cuda")
13 print(net(x).shape)

Launch on two CUDA GPUs with torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=2 tp_demo.py. Requires compatible PyTorch distributed APIs and two GPUs.

A paired ColwiseParallel and RowwiseParallel plan shards the two Linear layers across the same GPU group.

questions.stem: What communication and performance trade-offs occur when increasing Tensor Parallelism across GPUs, especially with all-reduce, all-gather, and slower network links?
options: Tensor Parallelism reduces memory per GPU and always improves throughput as more devices join, because all-reduce and all-gather exchange only tiny control messages. Network bandwidth has almost no impact once the model weights are distributed.

Tensor Parallelism partitions the layer and can use all-reduce to sum outputs, but all-gather replaces every synchronization step with local reads. Increasing GPU count removes collective communication bottlenecks instead of creating additional overhead in practice.

Tensor Parallelism needs collective communication, but its cost depends only on model parameter count, not tensor size, network topology, or link latency. Scaling performance should therefore be evaluated using GPU memory alone.

Tensor Parallelism spreads layer computation and weights across GPUs, but all-reduce and all-gather move partial results between devices. More shards can reduce local work while increasing synchronization costs, so interconnect speed and measured throughput matter.
questions.explanation: Explanation: TP can lower the memory and computation needed on each GPU, but ranks still exchange intermediate values. All-reduce sums partial results, and all-gather assembles distributed pieces. Both consume bandwidth and may introduce waiting time. For example, eight GPUs connected by fast links inside one server can behave differently from GPUs spread across slower network links. More shards are helpful only when saved local work outweighs communication; measure step time, collective time, memory, and actual throughput.

questions.stem: How can Tensor Parallelism be combined with Data Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism for large-model training, and what should engineers verify for reliable operation?
options: Use Tensor Parallelism within large layers, Pipeline Parallelism across groups of layers, and Data Parallelism across training batches. Verify shard shapes, gradient agreement, collective ordering, checkpoint recovery, memory, and throughput before expanding the distributed job.

Combine Tensor Parallelism by dividing data batches, Pipeline Parallelism by replicating all layers, and Data Parallelism by sharding individual matrices. Validate only training loss, since every GPU computes a complete independent network.

Use Tensor Parallelism inside layers and Pipeline Parallelism across stages, but run each Data Parallelism group with unrelated model weights and no gradient synchronization. Merge independently trained checkpoints after training to obtain an equivalent final model with stable results.

Combine all three strategies across GPUs, then assess success from high GPU utilization alone. Even mismatched collective calls or missing checkpoint shards can be ignored because the distributed system will automatically recover an identical model across training restarts.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A large training job may use TP for wide layers, Pipeline Parallelism for depth, and Data Parallelism for batches. For example, a 32-GPU training layout could have TP=2, PP=4 and DP=4. Engineers should verify feature shard shapes, compare loss and gradients with a smaller reference, ensure collective operations run in compatible order, and test checkpoint restoration before scaling. Also track memory, communication time and throughput. A fast training run is not useful if model results or checkpoints are incorrect.
